```{r setup}
library(healthexpectancies)
```

The package calculates **health expectancies**, and in particular disability-free life expectancies, with the Sullivan method. It also smooths prevalences of disability observed by age bracket, and projects prevalences and health expectancies. This vignette walks through a typical workflow, step by step:

1. calculating life expectancies with and without disability with `CompleteDFLEtable()`;
2. converting prevalences observed by age bracket into prevalences by single year of age with `ApproxPrevalenceTable()`;
3. projecting prevalences under simple hypotheses on life expectancies with `prevalenceForecast()`;
4. projecting prevalences with models estimated on past observations, with `fitPrevalenceModel()`, `predict()` and `projectPrevalence()`.

The methods of step 4 are described in detail in the vignette `vignette("projection-methods", package = "healthexpectancies")`. The last section lists the datasets included in the package.

# 1. Health expectancies with the Sullivan method

## Indicators

Three life expectancies at age $x$ are used throughout the package:

| Indicator | Meaning | Variable |
|---|---|---|
| total life expectancy | expected number of years lived | `ex` |
| disability-free life expectancy (DFLE) | expected number of years lived *without* disability (*espérance de vie sans incapacité*, EVSI, in French) | `DFLEx` |
| disability life expectancy (DLE) | expected number of years lived *with* disability (*espérance de vie en incapacité*, EVI, in French) | `DLEx` |

They add up: `ex = DFLEx + DLEx`. The shares of DFLE and DLE in total life expectancy are `pctDFLEx` and `pctDLEx` (in percent).

The Sullivan method combines a life table with the prevalence of disability at each age (`pix`, a proportion between 0 and 1): the person-years lived at each age are split into years lived with and without disability according to the prevalence at this age, and then summed over the following ages.

## `CompleteDFLEtable()`

`CompleteDFLEtable()` takes a data frame with at least the variables `age`, `qx` (probability of death between age $x$ and $x+1$) or `mx` (central death rate), and `pix`. It returns the same data frame, completed with all the variables of the life table and the health expectancies. If `pix` is missing, only total life expectancy is calculated.

The package includes the first example of the Sullivan manual (`sullivan`), which `CompleteDFLEtable()` reproduces:

```{r sullivan}
res <- CompleteDFLEtable(sullivan[, c("year", "age", "mx", "qx", "pix")])

# life expectancies at birth, at 65 and at 85
res[res$age %in% c(0, 65, 85), c("age", "ex", "DFLEx", "DLEx", "pctDFLEx")]
```

The meaning of each variable of the output is given in the dataset `description_sullivan`:

```{r description}
description_sullivan
```

## Several series at once

If the input data frame contains the variables `year` and/or `sex`, life expectancies are calculated separately for each year and sex. Other grouping variables (for instance a region or a social category) can be given with the argument `categories`. This is used in the next section, with two years.

# 2. From age brackets to single years of age

Prevalences of disability are usually observed by age bracket only (in surveys, sample sizes are too small to measure them at each age), whereas the Sullivan method needs prevalences by single year of age. `ApproxPrevalenceTable()` converts prevalences by bracket into smoothed prevalences by single year of age. By default, it minimises the second differences of the logit of prevalences, under the constraint that the average prevalence of each bracket, weighted by the population, is equal to the observed one.

The example uses the prevalence of the APA (*allocation personnalisée d'autonomie*, the French benefit for older people with long-term care needs), observed by 5-year age bracket from 60 to 85 and over (`FRAPAprevalence`).

```{r smoothing-data}
# Prevalences of the APA by age bracket, 2010 to 2024 (proportions)
apa <- FRAPAprevalence[FRAPAprevalence$decomp == 6, c("year", "age", "prevalence")]
head(apa)

# Population by single year of age (both sexes), used as weights.
# The population is measured on 1 January: the population on 1 January of year Y
# is the population at the end of year Y-1, like the prevalences of the APA.
pop <- FRInseePopulation[FRInseePopulation$geo == "france" &
                           FRInseePopulation$age0101 %in% 60:99, ]
pop$year <- pop$year - 1
pop <- aggregate(popx ~ year + age0101, data = pop, FUN = sum)
names(pop) <- c("year", "age", "popx")
```

```{r smoothing}
pix <- ApproxPrevalenceTable(apa,
                             agecuts     = seq(60, 85, 5),   # lower bounds of the brackets
                             agemin      = 60,
                             agemax      = 99,
                             weights.tab = pop,
                             categories  = "year")

# one row per year and single year of age, with the observed prevalence
# of the bracket (prevalence.raw) and the smoothed prevalence (prevalence.approx)
head(pix)
```

```{r fig-smoothing, fig.cap = "Prevalence of the APA in 2019: observed by age bracket (steps) and smoothed by single year of age (line)."}
p19 <- pix[pix$year == 2019, ]

plot(p19$age, p19$prevalence.raw,
     type = "s", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Age", ylab = "Prevalence of the APA")
lines(p19$age, p19$prevalence.approx, lwd = 2, col = "#0072B2")
legend("topleft", bty = "n", lwd = 2, col = c("black", "#0072B2"),
       legend = c("Observed, by age bracket", "Smoothed, by single year of age"))
```

## Health expectancies of the APA

To calculate life expectancies, the prevalences are merged with mortality rates. `FRInseeMortalityForecast2026` contains the mortality rates observed until 2022 and projected by Insee afterwards. The life table stops at age 104, where the probability of death is set to 1, and prevalences after age 99 are set equal to the prevalence at 99.

```{r le-apa}
# keep year, age and smoothed prevalence
pix <- data.frame(year = as.numeric(pix$year),
                  age  = pix$age,
                  pix  = pix$prevalence.approx)

# extension to ages 100-104 (same prevalence as at age 99)
last <- pix[pix$age == 99, ]
pix  <- rbind(pix, do.call(rbind, lapply(100:104, function(a) transform(last, age = a))))

# mortality rates, both sexes, ages 60 to 104
mort <- FRInseeMortalityForecast2026
mort <- mort[mort$sex == "all" &
               mort$geo %in% c("France excluding Mayotte", "France") &
               mort$def.age == "current age (approx)" &
               mort$age %in% 60:104,
             c("year", "age", "qx")]
mort$qx[mort$age == 104] <- 1

# life expectancies in 2010 and 2019
tab <- merge(pix[pix$year %in% c(2010, 2019), ], mort, by = c("year", "age"))
le  <- CompleteDFLEtable(tab)

le[le$age %in% c(60, 75, 85), c("year", "age", "ex", "DFLEx", "DLEx", "pctDLEx")]
```

Here, the "disability" is being a beneficiary of the APA: `DLEx` is the expected number of years spent as a beneficiary after age $x$. Between 2010 and 2019, total life expectancy at 60 increased, while the expected number of years spent as a beneficiary remained stable: the share of life expectancy at 60 spent as a beneficiary decreased.

# 3. Projections under simple hypotheses on life expectancies

`prevalenceForecast()` projects prevalences from a reference year, given projected mortality rates and a hypothesis on the evolution of health expectancies:

* `"cstPreval"`: prevalences by age remain constant;
* `"cstDFLE"`: DFLE remains constant at each age, so that all the gains in life expectancy are spent with disability;
* `"cstDLE"`: DLE remains constant at each age, so that all the gains in life expectancy are spent without disability;
* `"cstPctDFLE"` or `"cstPctDLE"`: the share of DFLE (or of DLE) in total life expectancy remains constant at each age (the two hypotheses are equivalent).

With the hypotheses on life expectancies, prevalences are obtained by *inverting* the Sullivan method. At the youngest ages, where prevalences are very low, this inversion can require negative prevalences: the argument `on_unfeasible = "clip"` bounds them to the interval 0 to 1 (with a warning), and recalculates life expectancies accordingly.

```{r forecast, warning = FALSE}
# reference year 2019, projections for 2030 and 2040
tabref  <- tab[tab$year == 2019, ]
tabproj <- mort[mort$year %in% c(2030, 2040), ]

hypotheses <- c("cstPreval", "cstDFLE", "cstDLE", "cstPctDLE")

fc <- do.call(rbind, lapply(hypotheses, function(h) {
  f <- prevalenceForecast(tabref, tabproj, hypo = h, on_unfeasible = "clip")
  f <- f[f$age == 60 & f$year == 2040, c("year", "ex", "DFLEx", "DLEx")]
  data.frame(hypothesis = h, f)
}))

fc
```

The four hypotheses give the same total life expectancy at 60 in 2040, since mortality is the same, but different numbers of years spent as a beneficiary of the APA.

# 4. Projections with models estimated on past observations

Instead of setting a hypothesis directly, `fitPrevalenceModel()` estimates a model of the evolution of prevalences on past years, and `predict()` uses it to project prevalences. Four families of methods are available:

* `method = "trend"`: extrapolation of the trend of (the logit of) prevalences, at each age;
* `method = "mortality"`: link between prevalences and mortality rates (possibly with an age shift);
* `method = "target"`: hypotheses on life expectancies (constant value, linear trend, or change of a given percentage at a given horizon), estimated on past years;
* `method = "shift"`: shift of the curve of prevalences towards older ages at a constant speed.

`projectPrevalence()` estimates the model, projects prevalences and calculates life expectancies in one step. The example below extrapolates the trend of the logit of prevalences at each age, estimated on 2010-2019 (the years of the Covid-19 epidemic are left out):

The projected prevalences are used to calculate life expectancies, so the model must cover all the ages of the life table: here, it is estimated on ages 60 to 104 (prevalences after age 99 being equal to the prevalence at 99). Since the projection goes far beyond the estimation period, `predict()` warns that the trend is extrapolated over a long horizon (the warning is not displayed here).

```{r project, warning = FALSE}
# estimation table: prevalences by single year of age (60 to 104), 2010 to 2019
obs <- pix[pix$year %in% 2010:2019, ]

# projection years: mortality rates up to the last age of the life table
newdata <- mort[mort$year %in% c(2030, 2040), ]

proj <- projectPrevalence(obs, newdata = newdata, method = "trend", fit_years = 2010:2019)

proj[proj$age == 60, c("year", "ex", "DFLEx", "DLEx", "pctDLEx")]
```

The estimated model is kept as an attribute of the result, and its results are available with the usual methods (`coef()`, `fitted()`, `residuals()`, `summary()`, `as.data.frame()`):

```{r model}
model <- attr(proj, "model")
model
```

The assumptions of each method, their limits and a comparison on the example of the APA are given in `vignette("projection-methods", package = "healthexpectancies")`.

# 5. Interactive example

The package includes a Shiny app, which illustrates projections of prevalences under the hypotheses of `prevalenceForecast()`. It requires the packages `shiny`, `shinydashboard`, `plotly` and `tidyverse`, which are not needed to install the package itself:

```{r shiny, eval = FALSE}
runExample()
```

# 6. Datasets included in the package

All the datasets, except `sullivan` and `description_sullivan`, concern France. Their full description is available in their help pages (for instance `?FRAPAprevalence`).

| Dataset | Content |
|---|---|
| `sullivan`, `description_sullivan` | first example of the Sullivan manual, and description of the variables of the output of `CompleteDFLEtable()` |
| **Prevalences** | |
| `FRAPAprevalence` | prevalence of the APA by age bracket, all sexes, 2010-2024 (DREES, *Aide sociale* survey) |
| `FRDreesAPA` | share of beneficiaries of the APA by sex and age bracket, at home and in institutions, 2016-2024 (DREES) |
| `FRDreesAPA2017` | share of beneficiaries of the APA by sex and age bracket, 2017 (DREES) |
| `FRDreesVQSsurvey2014`, `FRDreesVQSsurvey2021` | prevalences of disabilities by sex and age bracket, from the *Vie quotidienne et santé* (VQS) surveys of 2014 and 2021 (DREES) |
| `FRGaliEUSilc` | prevalence of general activity limitations (GALI) by sex and age bracket (SRCV survey, French part of EU-SILC) |
| `FRDreesEHPA` | share of people living in institutions for older people by sex and age (DREES, EHPA survey) |
| **Population** | |
| `FRInseePopulation` | population by sex and age on 1 January (Insee annual estimates) |
| `FRInseePopulationForecast2016`, `FRInseePopulationForecast2021`, `FRInseePopulationForecast2026` | population projections of Insee (central scenario) |
| **Mortality** | |
| `FRInseeMortalityrates`, `FRInseeMortalityrates_t69` | observed mortality rates by sex and age (Insee) |
| `FRInseeMortalityForecast2016`, `FRInseeMortalityForecast2021`, `FRInseeMortalityForecast2026` | observed and projected mortality rates by sex and age, from the population projections of Insee (central scenario) |
